chapters.file: ch14 - The Great Ecstasy of Werner Herzog Truth, Heidegger, Apocalypse.md
chapters.relation: Ian Alexander Moore reads Herzog's 'ecstatic truth' through Heidegger's account of truth as aletheia (unconcealment) and 'The Origin of the Work of Art,' arguing that Herzog's fabricated Pascal epigraph and Wagner Prelude in Lessons of Darkness and Lo and Behold elevate viewers into a sublime, ecstatic state that discloses a truth beyond the 'accountant's' factual. He connects the slow-motion ski-jumps of The Great Ecstasy of Woodcarver Steiner to Heidegger's ecstatic standing-outside-oneself, and treats Lessons of Darkness's burning Kuwaiti oil fields as an apocalyptic un-covering. He also warns that planetary information technology (echoing Heidegger's Question Concerning Technology) threatens the very oblivion of ecstatic truth.

chapters.file: ch15 - The Film Artist as Discoverer of the Marvels of Everyday Life a Kracauerian Reading of Werner Herzog.md
chapters.relation: Christopher Turner reads Herzog through Siegfried Kracauer's Theory of Film, arguing that Herzog, like Kracauer's 'film artist as explorer,' redeems physical reality by transfiguring the boring, habitual everyday into marvels. Herzog's warning about the extinction-level 'lack of adequate imagery' is aligned with Kracauer's redemption of the familiar, and films like Land of Silence and Darkness (deaf-blind Fini Straubinger) and Even Dwarfs Started Small reveal 'the unfamiliar in the familiar.' Turner invokes Benjamin (via Miriam Hansen) on the modern decline of Erfahrung into isolated Erlebnis to frame Herzog's discovery of a deeper, mysterious physical reality obscured by scientific abstraction.

chapters.file: ch16 - Werner Herzog and the Documentary as a Revelatory Practice.md
chapters.relation: Antony Fredriksson argues that Herzog's documentaries are not veridical fact-representations but a 'revelatory practice,' aligning Herzog's ecstatic-versus-accountant's-truth distinction with phenomenology (Merleau-Ponty, Husserl, Waldenfels). Using Merleau-Ponty's reading of Fabrice at Waterloo, he claims lived experience is contingent and pre-narrative, and that films like La Soufriere (a catastrophe that never happens), White Diamond (swifts behind the waterfall), and Echoes from a Somber Empire (the nicotine-addicted monkey) reveal the alien, attention-grabbing world beyond habitual seeing — a 'pathos' that reads the viewer rather than neutrally recording facts.

chapters.file: ch17 - On Experience and Illumination Werner Herzog’s Dialectical Relationship with Society.md
chapters.relation: Stefanie Baumann reads Herzog's attack on the 'accountant's truth' of the Minnesota Declaration alongside Horkheimer and Adorno's critical theory, arguing that the cult of facts reifies perception, creates norms, and serves the 'administered world' via the culture industry. She contends Herzog's films (Lessons of Darkness, Fata Morgana, Aguirre, The Enigma of Kaspar Hauser) resist this not by escaping society but by dialectically mediating singular, uncategorizable outsiders through the historically developed social order — Kaspar Hauser's 'obstinate otherness' exposing the social violence of enforced assimilation, a subversive constellation rather than an explicit political message.

Will Lehman argues that beneath Herzog's rejection of any guiding philosophy lies a 'masculinism' that exalts traditionally manly traits (courage, strength, independence, emotional control) as the heroic. Drawing on gender theory (Dozier on beards and the performance of gender), he shows Herzog fetishizing 'manly men,' reading illiteracy and calloused hands as authentic manhood (Jared Talbert in Into the Abyss), and coding even his female subject Juliane Koepcke (Wings of Hope) in masculine terms. Lehman reads Herzog's reenactment 'therapy' with Dengler and Dorrington as an assertion of dominance, while noting Herzog avoids overt misogyny or homophobia.

Anthony Eagan and Simon Thornton apply Kierkegaard's theory of tragedy (from the aesthete 'A' in Either/Or, plus the demonic in The Sickness unto Death) to argue that Timothy Treadwell (Grizzly Man) and Aguirre (Aguirre, the Wrath of God) are not tragic but comic figures. Both cross Herzog's 'invisible borderline' by asserting pure subjectivity over fate, romanticizing nature while ignoring the ambiguous collision of freedom and necessity that constitutes genuine tragedy. Treadwell freely engineers his own preventable death (so it cannot be tragic pain), and Aguirre, drifting in circles as self-proclaimed wrath of God, personifies the demonic refusal to repent — a 'post-tragic' comedy that aches.

chapters.file: ch20 - Werner Herzog on Circles, Chickens and Impotency.md
chapters.relation: Tyler Tritten argues that Even Dwarfs Started Small and Stroszek are not principally political but share an essence: the impotency of the powerless dramatized through cyclical, repetitive motion (circling trucks, ski lifts, and above all chickens). He defends Herzog's 'apoliticism' — citing Herzog's preference for the medieval melior pars over numerical voting (echoing Rousseau's general will versus the popular vote, and Socrates against the many) — as locating the human condition beneath contingent social conditions. The handless, cannibalistic, circumambulating chicken becomes the emblem of a self-consuming nature and a humanity too proportionate to the beast, provoking a pure, aching laughter as the only revolt.

holes.name: Aletheia (Truth as Unconcealment)
holes.what: Heidegger's conception of truth as a-letheia, an event of un-concealment or disclosure that precedes and grounds the correspondence theory of truth.
holes.why: Chapter 14's entire argument turns on Heidegger's aletheia as the philosophical key to Herzog's 'ecstatic truth,' and no taxonomy concept names truth-as-unconcealment (the existing Heidegger concepts cover authenticity, technology, das Man, being-toward-death, thrownness, Dasein, not aletheia).

holes.name: Siegfried Kracauer
holes.what: Weimar-era film theorist and Frankfurt-School-adjacent critic whose Theory of Film argues cinema 'redeems physical reality' by revealing the marvels of everyday life.
holes.why: Chapter 15 is a sustained Kracauerian reading of Herzog built almost entirely on Kracauer's film theory, but Kracauer appears nowhere in the taxonomy's philosopher list.

holes.name: Max Horkheimer
holes.what: Co-founder of the Frankfurt School whose Eclipse of Reason and (with Adorno) Dialectic of Enlightenment critique instrumental reason, the concept of the 'fact,' and the administered world.
holes.why: Chapter 17 develops its critique of factual truth jointly through Horkheimer and Adorno, quoting Horkheimer extensively, yet only Adorno (and not Horkheimer) exists in the taxonomy.

holes.name: Masculinism (glorification of manliness)
holes.what: The exaltation and promotion of traits traditionally subsumed under 'manliness' (courage, strength, independence, emotional control) as heroic ideals, distinct from men's-rights masculism.
holes.why: Chapter 18's thesis is explicitly that Herzog holds a 'philosophy of masculinism,' and the taxonomy's gender concepts (gender-performativity, objectification, male-gaze, five-faces-oppression) name critiques of gendered power but not the affirmative glorification of masculinity the chapter analyzes.

holes.name: Kierkegaard on the Tragic (ancient vs. modern) and the Comic
holes.what: The aesthete 'A''s theory in Either/Or that tragedy requires an ambiguity between freedom/guilt and fate/suffering, and that a modern age of pure subjectivity collapses the tragic into the comic.
holes.why: Chapter 19's 'post-tragic aesthetic' rests specifically on Kierkegaard's theory of tragedy and the comic, which no existing Kierkegaard concept (leap-of-faith, stages, despair, anxiety, teleological suspension, subjective truth) captures.
